chapter_summary:
Effective performance optimization begins with robust monitoring. Without a clear understanding of your system's behavior, identifying bottlenecks and areas for improvement becomes a guessing game. AWS CloudWatch serves as the foundational monitoring service, collecting metrics, logs, and events from virtually all AWS services. For a professional architect, simply enabling basic CloudWatch metrics is insufficient. We must dive deeper into custom metrics, advanced alarming, and sophisticated log analysis to gain true observability into complex, multi-tier applications.

Custom metrics are powerful because they allow you to track application-specific performance indicators that AWS intrinsic metrics might miss. For instance, you might want to monitor the number of items processed by a specific Lambda function per minute, the latency of a particular API call within your application code, or the depth of a custom message queue. To publish a custom metric, you typically use the AWS CLI or SDK within your application code or a dedicated monitoring agent. The `aws cloudwatch put-metric-data` command is your primary tool here. You define a namespace, a metric name, a value, and optionally dimensions. Dimensions are key-value pairs that allow you to slice and dice your metric data, providing granular insights. For example, a `Latency` metric could have `FunctionName` and `APIName` dimensions, allowing you to filter latency by specific Lambda functions or API endpoints. It's crucial to choose appropriate dimensions, as each unique combination of dimensions for a metric incurs cost. Over-dimensioning can lead to unnecessary expense and complexity.

```bash
# Example: Publishing a custom metric for API latency
aws cloudwatch put-metric-data \
  --metric-name APILatency \
  --namespace "MyApplication/API" \
  --value 150 \
  --dimensions Service=UserService,Endpoint=/users/{id} \
  --unit Milliseconds
```

Once metrics are collected, CloudWatch Alarms become critical for proactive issue detection. Beyond simple threshold alarms, professional architects leverage composite alarms and metric math. Metric math allows you to perform calculations on multiple metrics, creating new metrics that represent more complex system states. For example, you could calculate the error rate of an application by dividing the `Errors` metric by the `Invocations` metric for a Lambda function. This derived metric provides a more meaningful signal than just monitoring raw error counts, especially as traffic fluctuates. Composite alarms, on the other hand, allow you to combine multiple simple alarms into a single, more intelligent alarm. This is invaluable for reducing alert fatigue. Instead of receiving separate alerts for high CPU, low memory, and high disk I/O on an EC2 instance, you could create a composite alarm that triggers only when *two or more* of these conditions are met, indicating a more severe problem. This helps in distinguishing between transient spikes and genuine performance degradations.

For large-scale organizations, managing monitoring across multiple AWS accounts and regions is a common challenge. CloudWatch offers solutions for this, primarily through cross-account observability. You can configure a monitoring account (sink account) to aggregate metrics, logs, and traces from multiple source accounts. This provides a centralized view of your entire AWS estate, simplifying operations and compliance. For metrics, you can use `PutMetricData` from source accounts to the monitoring account, or more commonly, use CloudWatch cross-account metric sharing. Similarly, for logs, Kinesis Data Firehose can be used to stream logs from various accounts into a central S3 bucket or CloudWatch Logs in the monitoring account, where CloudWatch Logs Insights can then query across all aggregated log groups.

CloudWatch Logs Insights is an incredibly powerful, interactive query language for analyzing your log data. Instead of sifting through raw log files, you can use SQL-like queries to extract, filter, and aggregate log events. This is indispensable for troubleshooting. For example, you can quickly find all error messages for a specific request ID, identify the slowest database queries, or count occurrences of a particular pattern across millions of log lines. Mastering Logs Insights significantly reduces the time to diagnose issues. Common mistakes include not parsing log fields correctly or writing inefficient queries. Always ensure your application logs structured data (e.g., JSON) to make parsing easier.

```sql
# Example: CloudWatch Logs Insights query to find high-latency API requests
fields @timestamp, @message
| parse @message "latency: *ms" as latency
| filter latency > 500 and @message like /GET \/api\/v1\/users/
| sort by @timestamp desc
| limit 20
```

Finally, effective CloudWatch Dashboards are crucial for visualizing performance data. A well-designed dashboard provides a quick, high-level overview of your system's health, allowing you to spot trends and anomalies at a glance. For professional architects, dashboards should not just display raw metrics; they should tell a story. Group related metrics, use appropriate visualization types (line graphs for trends, bar charts for comparisons, numbers for key performance indicators), and arrange widgets logically. Consider creating specialized dashboards for different audiences or purposes: an operational dashboard for real-time alerts, a business dashboard for key performance indicators (KPIs), and a troubleshooting dashboard with more granular metrics. Common mistakes include creating cluttered dashboards with too many irrelevant metrics or failing to include context like alarm states directly on the dashboard. Always include alarm status widgets alongside the metrics they monitor.

screens.title: Introduction to Performance Metrics & Monitoring
screens.subtitle: Why observability is the foundation of performance optimization

narration.text: Observability is the lens through which you understand a distributed system's behavior. In this chapter you'll learn how CloudWatch collects metrics, logs, and events and how advanced features—custom metrics, metric math, composite alarms, and Logs Insights—turn raw data into actionable signals. We'll use concrete examples such as publishing custom latency metrics from a Lambda function, deriving error rates with metric math, and building a composite alarm that reduces alert fatigue. You'll also see practical cross-account patterns to centralize monitoring for multi-account organizations, and how to design dashboards that tell a clear operational story. By the end you will understand not only how to configure these features, but why each choice—namespaces, dimensions, aggregation intervals, and dashboard widgets—affects signal quality, cost, and response time. A brief hands-on activity walks you through instrumenting a sample OrderProcessor Lambda and creating alarms, so you can practice publishing metrics and observing their effect. Consider an incident you've seen: as we progress, notice which metric or log line would have revealed the root cause sooner.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Effective performance optimization relies on tailored metrics and smart alarms. Raw metrics must be transformed into meaningful signals to find bottlenecks quickly and reduce noisy alerts.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will practice in this chapter

narration.text: In this chapter you will develop four core competencies that professional architects use daily. First, you will articulate why comprehensive monitoring and observability are essential: this includes distinguishing telemetry types and understanding how observability reduces mean time to resolution. Second, you will configure and interpret advanced CloudWatch features including custom metrics, metric math, and composite alarms; you'll practice choosing namespaces and dimensions and see how derived metrics like error rates improve signal quality. Third, you will implement cross-account and cross-region monitoring strategies: centralizing metrics and logs into a monitoring account reduces operational overhead for multi-account organizations while preserving isolation. Fourth, you will use CloudWatch Logs Insights effectively for interactive log analysis to find root causes quickly and to design dashboards that present real-time performance. Each objective includes a practical milestone so you can verify competency: publishing a custom metric, creating a metric math expression, configuring cross-account metric sharing, and writing a Logs Insights query to find high-latency requests. These skills matter because they move you from reactive firefighting to proactive system design. Consider which objective will most reduce noise in your team's current alerting.

keyIdea.text: Build observable systems by publishing meaningful metrics, deriving signals with metric math, centralizing monitoring, and analyzing logs with Logs Insights.

screens.title: Why comprehensive monitoring matters
screens.subtitle: From guessing to evidence-driven performance work

narration.text: Monitoring is not an operational ornament; it is the evidence you need to prioritize performance work. In distributed systems you cannot rely on single indicators: C P U or request counts alone will not reveal queuing delays, downstream latency, or sporadic application errors. CloudWatch collects telemetry—metrics, logs, and events—that together provide a multidimensional view. Metrics reveal trends and aggregate health, logs provide the detailed diagnostic context, and events or traces explain causal sequences. For a professional architect, the key skill is choosing which signals become part of your operational story. A common mistake is to accept default metrics and alarms; this creates blind spots. Instead, define custom metrics for business and application-level indicators such as items processed per minute or end-to-end latency. Use dimensions to slice by service or endpoint, but avoid needless dimension explosion because each unique combination increases storage and cost. For example, tracking A P I latency with dimensions service and endpoint helps you compare endpoints, but adding user-id as a dimension will produce high-cardinality metrics that are expensive and rarely useful. The practical takeaway: design telemetry to answer the recurrent questions your team asks during incidents—what is slow, where is the error, and which user flows are affected. As you instrument, ask whether a single metric will meaningfully change your response, and prefer derived signals when raw counters are misleading.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Monitoring must be targeted: choose metrics and logs that answer operational questions and enable quick diagnosis.

content.html:
Core Concept
Why comprehensive monitoring matters
Monitoring turns unknowns into measurable signals you can act on.
What to track
  • Business indicators (throughput, processed items)
  • Application metrics (latency, error counts)
  • Infrastructure metrics (CPU, memory) for resource issues
Misconception
Relying only on built-in metrics misses application-level failures. Default alarms often produce false positives.
Key Takeaway

Design telemetry to answer real incident questions; prefer derived signals to raw counts when traffic varies.

Analogy: medical diagnostics
Just as doctors use vitals, blood tests, and imaging, architects combine metrics, logs, and traces to diagnose system health.
Scenario card
Unexpected latency during peak
Use a custom latency metric and Logs Insights to determine whether a downstream database or an internal API caused the spike.
Common mistake
Alerting on raw error counts without context leads to alert storms during traffic spikes.
Pro tip
Choose dimensions that slice meaningful operational groups like service or endpoint, not high-cardinality identifiers.

narration.text: CloudWatch acts as the central telemetry store for AWS services: it ingests metrics, logs, and events. Metrics are numeric time-series data points that summarize state over a fixed period; they are efficient for trend analysis and alarms. Logs are raw or structured text records you can query interactively with Logs Insights to find the precise lines that explain an event. Events capture discrete occurrences such as state changes or scheduled tasks. For advanced monitoring you will rely on all three. Metrics give you the early signal, Logs Insights gives you root cause detail, and events help you correlate state transitions. One important concept is namespaces: a namespace groups related metrics, often by application or team, preventing name collisions. Dimensions attach context to a metric; they are key-value pairs such as ServiceName or Endpoint. Proper use of dimensions lets you filter and compare, but overuse creates cardinality and cost. An additional practical note: CloudWatch usage model includes costs for custom metrics and high-resolution metrics. A common misconception is that more metrics always improve troubleshooting; in practice, thoughtful metric design balances actionable fidelity with cost. Example: publish a single OrderProcessingTime metric with ServiceName and not user-id to keep cardinality low while still supporting operational slices.

keyIdea.title: Telemetry model
keyIdea.text: Use metrics for trends and alarms, logs for root cause, and events for correlation. Use namespaces and dimensions to organize telemetry while controlling cardinality.

content.html:
Definition
CloudWatch telemetry model
Metrics, logs, and events serve distinct troubleshooting roles.
Namespaces
Group metrics (for example, MyApplication/Orders) so related metrics don't collide.
Dimensions
Attach key-value pairs like ServiceName and Endpoint to filter and compare metrics.
Cardinality caution
Avoid high-cardinality dimensions such as user IDs unless necessary for a targeted analysis.
Examples
Built-in metric
Lambda Duration provides average or p99 durations out of the box.
Custom metric
OrderProcessingTime in namespace MyApplication/Orders with dimension ServiceName=OrderProcessorService.
Why this matters

Clear telemetry boundaries make dashboards and alarms reliable and easier to interpret during incidents.

screens.title: Publishing custom metrics (CLI & SDK)
screens.subtitle: How to publish application-specific metrics and choose dimensions

narration.text: Custom metrics let you track application-level indicators that built-in metrics miss. To publish a metric, you use the put-metric-data operation from the CLI or an SDK inside your application. Essential fields are namespace, metric name, value, unit, and optional dimensions which let you slice the metric. A concrete example: measure A P I latency for a UserService endpoint and publish it with dimensions Service=UserService and Endpoint=/users/{id}. Using the CLI you might call the put-metric-data command with a namespace like MyApplication/A P I. In code you typically capture duration and call the SDK client to put the metric as part of request handling. Be mindful of dimension choice: include service and endpoint, but avoid per-request identifiers. Another practical point: set an appropriate resolution and aggregation period so alarms behave predictably—one-minute aggregation is common for latency. Common mistakes include sending too many unique dimension values and publishing a metric per request without aggregation, which inflates costs and makes charts noisy. Walk through a short example from the activity: the OrderProcessor Lambda publishes OrderProcessingTime and OrderProcessingErrors under MyApplication/Orders. Verify the metric appears in CloudWatch after invoking the Lambda several times. This verification confirms both data ingestion and proper dimension labeling.

keyIdea.title: Publish tips
keyIdea.text: Use namespaces and a small set of operationally meaningful dimensions, and verify ingestion by invoking the instrumented code and viewing the metric.

content.html:
Process
Publishing custom metrics
Use the CLI or SDK to send application-specific telemetry.
CLI example
aws cloudwatch put-metric-data \
  --metric-name APILatency \
  --namespace "MyApplication/API" \
  --value 150 \
  --dimensions Service=UserService,Endpoint=/users/{id} \
  --unit Milliseconds
This command publishes a single datapoint. Repeat or batch from the application depending on your SDK and design.
In-code pattern (Python)
# inside request handler
start = time.time()
# handle request
duration = (time.time() - start) * 1000
cloudwatch.put_metric_data(
  Namespace='MyApplication/Orders',
  MetricData=[{
    'MetricName': 'OrderProcessingTime',
    'Dimensions':[{'Name':'ServiceName','Value':'OrderProcessorService'}],
    'Value': duration,
    'Unit':'Milliseconds'
  }]
)
Verify by invoking the function multiple times and checking CloudWatch for the namespace and dimensions you selected.
Design note
Batch metrics when possible, avoid per-request dimensional explosion, and choose aggregation periods that match your alerting cadence.

screens.title: Metric Math: deriving meaningful signals
screens.subtitle: Combine metrics with expressions to create actionable metrics

narration.text: Metric Math allows you to compute new metrics from existing ones using expressions. This is essential when raw counters are insufficient. A common use is computing an error rate by dividing Errors by Invocations or calculating combined latency across multiple services with sum or average expressions. Metric Math expressions call existing metrics by identifier, apply arithmetic, and can use functions such as SUM and AVG. Practically, you create the base metrics first—either built-in or custom—then define an expression like m1 / m2 to compute rates. You can then create an alarm on the expression itself. This is powerful because it keeps your alarm logic aligned with the derived meaning you care about, rather than raw counts that scale with traffic. A misconception is that Metric Math is just for visualization; in reality alarms can target expressions directly. When designing expressions, be explicit about the statistic used (Average, Sum) and the period to avoid misinterpreting aggregated values. For example, to detect combined latency exceeding one second for two Lambda functions, use the built-in Duration average for each and a Metric Math expression m1 + m2, then alarm on the expression for five consecutive minutes. Metric Math is precise and reduces extra processing outside CloudWatch.

keyIdea.title: Metric Math use
keyIdea.text: Derive ratios and sums from base metrics so alarms represent meaningful service-level conditions rather than raw counts.

content.html:
Process Flow
Metric Math: deriving meaningful signals
Create expressions to compute error rates, combined latency, or other derived metrics.
Steps
  1. Identify base metrics and their statistics (Average, Sum).
  2. Define a Metric Math expression such as m1 / m2 or m1 + m2.
  3. Visualize the expression and create an alarm targeting it directly.
Example: m1 = AuthService Duration (avg), m2 = PaymentService Duration (avg), expression = m1 + m2.
Example expression
// visualize combined average latency
m1 = Metric('AuthService','Duration',stat='Average')
m2 = Metric('PaymentService','Duration',stat='Average')
expression = m1 + m2
Create an alarm on the expression when the result stays above 1000 ms for 5 minutes. This approach directly maps to the operational requirement.
Misconception
Metric Math is only cosmetic. Actually you can alarm on expressions, which is the recommended path for combined signals.

screens.title: Composite Alarms: reduce alert fatigue
screens.subtitle: Combine simple alarms into stronger, actionable signals

narration.text: Composite Alarms let you combine the states of multiple alarms using logical operators so you only notify when a combination indicates a real problem. The idea is simple but powerful: instead of alerting on every single threshold breach, define a rule such as 'trigger only when two or more conditions are true' or a logical OR between critical alarms. For instance, you might have separate alarms for high C P U, high memory, and high disk input and output; a composite alarm can be configured to fire only when two of those alarms are in ALARM state, which helps separate transient spikes from sustained problems. Composite alarms reference existing simple alarms by name and evaluate according to the rule you provide; they do not duplicate metric data. A common mistake is creating composite alarms that are too permissive or too restrictive; test them by simulating alarm states. When combining with Metric Math, you can alert on a derived expression and then include that derived-alarm in composites. Use composite alarms to centralize critical paths: for the OrderProcessor scenario, combine high processing time and any error alarm into a CriticalOrderProcessorIssues composite alarm. This reduces noise and ensures responders only see high-confidence incidents.

keyIdea.title: Composite alarm pattern
keyIdea.text: Combine simple alarms with logical rules to notify on meaningful, multi-signal conditions and reduce alert fatigue.

content.html:
Process Flow
Composite Alarms
Group simple alarms into rules that represent meaningful failures.
Rule example
ALARM("HighProcessingTimeAlarm") OR ALARM("HighErrorRateAlarm") -> triggers CriticalOrderProcessorIssues.
Test composite alarms by forcing the underlying simple alarms into ALARM state to validate notification behavior and escalation paths.
Benefits
  • Reduce noisy alerts by requiring multiple signals
  • Encode operational judgment in alarm rules
  • Simplify on-call response with higher-confidence alerts
Common mistake
Relying on a single composite rule for every situation. Instead, create targeted composites for critical workflows.

narration.text: At scale, teams operate across multiple AWS accounts and regions, so centralizing observability reduces friction and supports compliance. CloudWatch supports cross-account observability: configure a monitoring account as a sink to aggregate metrics and logs from source accounts. For metrics, you can use PutMetricData to send custom metrics into a monitoring account or use cross-account metric sharing features. For logs, many teams stream them via Kinesis Data Firehose to a central S3 bucket or to CloudWatch Logs in the monitoring account. This centralization enables a single dashboard to show health across Dev, Staging, and Prod, and simplifies alert routing to security or SRE teams. A key design decision is whether to aggregate raw logs or only derived metrics; raw logs give full context but increase storage cost and complexity. Another consideration is region boundaries: either replicate monitoring configurations per region or centralize by exporting to a single region—balance latency and compliance needs. Misconceptions include thinking cross-account observability removes the need for source-account alarms; don’t eliminate local alarms that provide rapid feedback. Instead, use the monitoring account for centralized correlation, auditing, and high-level dashboards while retaining local quick-response alarms where appropriate.

keyIdea.title: Central monitoring
keyIdea.text: Use a monitoring account to aggregate metrics and logs from multiple accounts, balancing completeness with cost and latency.

content.html:
Architecture
Cross-account observability
Centralize metrics and logs for compliance, correlation, and simpler dashboards.
Patterns
  • Metric sharing or PutMetricData into a monitoring account
  • Stream logs with Kinesis Data Firehose into central S3 or CloudWatch Logs
  • Build central dashboards and alert routing in the monitoring account
Design considerations
  • Storage costs vs. diagnostic completeness when aggregating raw logs
  • Region-specific compliance or latency constraints
  • Retain local alarms for fast response; use the monitoring account for correlation
Scenario
Security team needs failed login counts across Prod and Staging. Use cross-account metric sharing to a Security monitoring account and build a single dashboard.

screens.title: Aggregating logs for analysis
screens.subtitle: Streaming logs to a central store for Logs Insights

narration.text: Logs are indispensable for root-cause analysis, but raw logs scattered across accounts and regions slow investigations. A common pattern is to stream logs from source accounts into a central location using Kinesis Data Firehose. From there you can deliver logs to S3 or CloudWatch Logs in a monitoring account where Logs Insights queries can run across aggregated log groups. The advantages are clear: you can run consistent queries, retain a single compliance-backed archive, and reduce context switching. When designing streams, include identifying fields such as account or region in each log record so you can filter results during queries. Be mindful of costs: full log retention of verbose debug logs can be expensive, so tier retention by environment or log type. A frequent mistake is sending unstructured plaintext logs; prefer structured JSON logs so Logs Insights can parse fields easily and queries are more efficient. Also consider parsing at ingestion to extract common fields. By centralizing logs and keeping them structured, on-call engineers can write concise Logs Insights queries to find the highest-latency requests or the most frequent error messages across accounts quickly.

keyIdea.title: Log aggregation
keyIdea.text: Stream structured logs into a central monitoring account to enable efficient Logs Insights queries and consistent retention policies.

content.html:
Architecture
Aggregating logs for analysis
Stream logs from source accounts to a central store for consistent analysis.
Pattern
  • Use Kinesis Data Firehose to stream logs
  • Deliver to S3 for archive or to CloudWatch Logs in the monitoring account
  • Include account and region metadata in each record
Best practices
  • Log structured JSON to ease parsing and querying
  • Tier retention by environment to manage cost
  • Parse common fields at ingestion where possible
Example
Stream application logs to S3 and query them via Logs Insights in the monitoring account to find high-latency requests across multiple services.

screens.title: CloudWatch Logs Insights: query patterns
screens.subtitle: Use interactive queries to find high-latency requests and errors

narration.text: CloudWatch Logs Insights is an interactive query language designed to slice and aggregate log events quickly. The power of Logs Insights comes from parsing structured fields, filtering, aggregation, and sorting. A typical query pattern is: select relevant fields, parse the message to extract latency, filter by a threshold and a path, then sort by timestamp. For example, you can parse 'latency: *ms' into a latency field and filter latency greater than 500 ms for a specific A P I route. Logs Insights returns aggregates quickly even across millions of lines, which significantly reduces time to diagnose. An important tip is to ensure your application emits structured logs like JSON so you can use parse with field extraction directly instead of relying on brittle string parsing. Another efficiency note is to limit the time range and scope to relevant log groups to reduce query latency and cost. Common mistakes include over-scanning long retention periods or not indexing useful fields at emission. In practice: run a query to show the 20 most recent slow requests and then click through to the raw event for context. This is how you move from a metric spike to the exact log lines that reveal the root cause.

keyIdea.title: Logs Insights pattern
keyIdea.text: Parse structured logs, filter on thresholds, and aggregate to find the slowest requests or most frequent errors quickly.

content.html:
Definition
CloudWatch Logs Insights
An interactive query language for searching and aggregating logs.
Query example
fields @timestamp, @message
| parse @message "latency: *ms" as latency
| filter latency > 500 and @message like /GET \/api\/v1\/users/
| sort by @timestamp desc
| limit 20
This query finds recent high-latency GET requests to the users endpoint and returns the latest 20 matches.
Best practices
  • Structure logs as JSON to simplify parsing
  • Scope queries to relevant log groups and time ranges
  • Extract important fields like requestId and latency at emission
Check your understanding
If latency is present in multiple formats, ensure your parse covers variants or normalize at log emission.

screens.title: Designing effective CloudWatch dashboards
screens.subtitle: Which widgets to use and how to tell a clear operational story

narration.text: A dashboard should present a single operational story: it should help you answer whether the system is healthy, where anomalies are happening, and what to investigate next. Use visualization types deliberately: line graphs are best for trends and latency over time, stacked bars or bars for comparisons, and single-number widgets for immediate key performance indicators like current error rate or throughput. Group related metrics and widgets so viewers find context quickly. For example, an operational dashboard might group compute and memory charts for an application cluster, a separate row for business KPIs, and an alarm status widget positioned next to the graphs it monitors. A troubleshooting dashboard should surface detailed, high-cardinality metrics and Logs Insights widgets for quick drilling. Common mistakes include cluttering a dashboard with too many widgets or mixing unrelated KPIs; both reduce signal-to-noise. Also include alarm state widgets adjacent to the metric they relate to, so an engineer can see both the graph and the alarm. Finally, create different dashboards for different audiences: an executive dashboard with top-level KPIs and an on-call dashboard with narrow, actionable views. A well-designed dashboard shortens time to triage and focuses attention where it matters.

keyIdea.title: Dashboard design
keyIdea.text: Use widget types intentionally, group related metrics, and build audience-specific dashboards to surface the right signal.

content.html:
Comparison
Designing dashboards
Choose widget types and layout to tell a clear operational story.
Widget guidance
  • Line charts for trends and percentiles
  • Number widgets for KPIs like error rate
  • Logs Insights panels for drill-down queries
Layout patterns
  • Top row: critical KPIs and alarm states
  • Middle: service-level graphs grouped by application
  • Bottom: troubleshooting widgets and Logs Insights
Pro tip
Create separate dashboards for operations, business stakeholders, and incident response to keep views focused.

screens.title: Hands-on: instrumenting OrderProcessor Lambda
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: publish metrics and create alarms using the provided code

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through instrumenting the OrderProcessor Lambda to publish two custom metrics and then creating alarms and a composite alarm. Start by deploying the Lambda with the provided Python code that captures processing duration and a count of errors. Ensure the Lambda execution role includes cloudwatch:PutMetricData permission and set the environment variables CLOUDWATCH_NAMESPACE to MyApplication/Orders and SERVICE_NAME to OrderProcessorService. Invoke the function 20 to 30 times to generate metrics. Confirm in CloudWatch that OrderProcessingTime and OrderProcessingErrors appear under the namespace with the ServiceName dimension. Next create two alarms: one on OrderProcessingTime greater than 300 milliseconds for one datapoint over one minute, and another on OrderProcessingErrors greater than 0 for one datapoint over one minute. Finally, create a composite alarm named CriticalOrderProcessorIssues with the rule ALARM("HighProcessingTimeAlarm") OR ALARM("HighErrorRateAlarm") so it fires when either condition is met. Observe how the composite alarm reduces alert volume compared to separate notifications. A common pitfall is forgetting the metric namespace or using inconsistent dimension names, so verify both values exactly when testing. This activity ties configuration to observable outcomes and demonstrates how derived alerts improve operational focus.

keyIdea.title: Activity outcome
keyIdea.text: Instrument the Lambda, emit two custom metrics, create two alarms, and consolidate them into a composite alarm to observe improved alert quality.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Instrument OrderProcessor
Deploy the provided Lambda, ensure PutMetricData permission, set environment variables, then invoke repeatedly.
Lambda snippet
import time
import random
import boto3
cloudwatch = boto3.client('cloudwatch')
# publish OrderProcessingTime and OrderProcessingErrors to MyApplication/Orders
Alarm steps
  1. Create HighProcessingTime alarm on OrderProcessingTime > 300 ms for 1 datapoint, 1 minute.
  2. Create HighErrorRate alarm on OrderProcessingErrors > 0 for 1 datapoint, 1 minute.
  3. Create composite alarm CriticalOrderProcessorIssues with rule ALARM("HighProcessingTimeAlarm") OR ALARM("HighErrorRateAlarm").
Verification
Invoke the function, review the custom metrics in CloudWatch, and observe alarm state transitions in the console.

screens.title: Assessment: choosing the right approach
screens.subtitle: Apply metric math and cross-account patterns to a multi-service latency problem

narration.text: Assessment exercises test whether you can translate requirements into CloudWatch constructs. One representative question asks you to monitor average end-to-end latency across AuthService and PaymentService and alert when their combined average exceeds one second for five minutes. The correct approach is to use the built-in Duration metric for each Lambda, apply Metric Math to sum their averages, and create an alarm on the Metric Math expression. This is efficient and leverages native metrics without coupling services. A common wrong choice is to try to push one service to report another service’s latency which creates coupling and operational confusion. Another exercise asks how to centralize security metrics across Dev, Staging, and Prod; the recommended answer is to use cross-account metric sharing to a centralized Security account and build a dashboard there. When solving these problems, clearly state the metric names, namespaces, required dimensions, aggregation periods, and alarm evaluation windows. This shows you can map operational intent—detecting combined latency or consolidating security signals—into CloudWatch features. Finally, explain trade-offs: Metric Math uses existing metrics and supports alarms, while Logs Insights is better for ad-hoc troubleshooting but not for direct alarming.

keyIdea.title: Assessment guidance
keyIdea.text: Map operational requirements to CloudWatch features: use Metric Math for combined metrics and cross-account sharing for centralized dashboards.

content.html:
Assessment Idea
Choose the right approach
Translate an SLO or alerting requirement into metrics, expressions, and alarms.
What to include in your answer
  • Metric names and namespaces used
  • Dimensions and aggregation periods
  • Metric Math expression and alarm window
  • Trade-offs and edge cases
Sample solution summary
Use Duration (Average) for both Lambdas, expression m1 + m2, alarm on expression > 1000 ms for 5 minutes. For cross-account, use metric sharing to a Security monitoring account.
Pitfall
Do not attempt to create alarms directly from Logs Insights query results; Logs Insights is for interactive analysis, not primary alarming.

narration.text: Summarizing the chapter, remember these core ideas. First, CloudWatch is the center for metrics, logs, and events; choose namespaces and dimensions thoughtfully to balance sliceability and cost. Second, custom metrics are essential for application-level signals; publish them with proper dimensions and verify ingestion. Third, Metric Math enables you to derive meaningful signals, like error rates or combined latency, and you can create alarms on those expressions. Fourth, composite alarms reduce alert fatigue by combining multiple conditions into a higher-confidence signal. Fifth, cross-account observability centralizes monitoring across accounts and regions, but retain local alarms for fast feedback. Sixth, CloudWatch Logs Insights efficiently surfaces root-cause log lines when you emit structured logs. Finally, dashboards should tell a clear operational story and be tailored to the audience. These compact reminders capture the operational patterns that will make your systems observable and your team's response faster.

keyIdea.title: Chapter takeaway
keyIdea.text: Design telemetry for action: publish useful metrics, derive signals with Metric Math, reduce noise with composite alarms, and centralize observability where it adds value.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Key Concepts
CloudWatch
Collects metrics, logs, and events for observability.
Custom Metrics
Publish application-level indicators with namespaces and dimensions.
Metric Math
Compute derived metrics like error rates or combined latency and alarm on them.
Remember

Well-designed telemetry and alarm rules shorten detection and resolution times. Use the right tool for the question: metrics for trends, Logs Insights for root cause, composites for high-confidence alerts.

narration.text: End with three compact reminders you can act on immediately. First, choose metrics that map to operational questions and avoid high-cardinality dimensions. Second, use Metric Math and composite alarms so alerts reflect meaningful system states rather than raw counts. Third, centralize shared observability—but keep fast local alarms—so teams can both respond quickly and correlate issues across accounts. These three rules will help you create observability that is both actionable and maintainable. After this chapter, try instrumenting one service with a custom metric and create one Metric Math expression and a composite alarm to see the practical reduction in noise. What to Remember means 1) design metrics to answer operational questions. 2) derive signals and combine alarms for actionable alerts. 3) centralize observability while preserving local responsiveness.. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. keyIdea.text: 1) Design metrics to answer operational questions. 2) Derive signals and combine alarms for actionable alerts. 3) Centralize observability while preserving local responsiveness.

Metric design
Track business and app signals, limit cardinality, verify ingestion.
